Mohyliv-Podilskyy Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Vinnytska oblast, Ukraine

Demolished. Mohyliv-Podilskyi was named for the Moldavian prince Ieremia Movilă, who gave the town as a dowry when his daughter married into the powerful Polish Potocki family; it grew into the largest town in the historical region of Podillya and, remarkably for this collection, was a genuinely multi-ethnic border community of Poles, Greeks, Armenians, Serbs, Vlachs, Bosniaks, and Jews. Its Jewish community, documented from 1637, grew enormous — 5,411 by 1847, supporting 16 synagogues and prayer houses by 1867, and peaking at 12,344 (55 percent of the town) by 1897. During WWII, under Romanian administration as part of the Transnistria Governorate, the town became a transit camp of staggering scale: more than 55,000 Jewish deportees from Bessarabia and Bukovina passed through between September 1941 and February 1942 alone, most forced onward under brutal conditions, while a smaller group was permitted to remain in town under constant threat of further deportation. A small Jewish community with its own synagogue survives in Mohyliv-Podilskyi today — a rare continuity in this collection. This cemetery, believed founded in the 17th century, was demolished in the 1930s during the construction of a stadium, and its former site is now occupied by another cemetery.
